title: Empanadas de Carne
subtitle: Baked beef and olive empanadas
excerpt: Flaky hand-held pastries filled with spiced minced beef, olives and hard-boiled egg. This recipe makes 12 empanadas and takes about 70 minutes. They are eaten across Argentina at every occasion from family lunch to street food, and baked rather than fried for a lighter result.
sourceNotes: Empanadas arrived in Argentina via Spain, where they were brought from the Moorish tradition of stuffed pastries. Argentine empanadas developed their own distinct regional styles, with Salta-style being smaller and spicier and Buenos Aires style being larger and richer. They are eaten as street food, at asados and as a casual meal.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze assembled, unbaked empanadas on a tray, then transfer to a bag. Bake from frozen at 200C for 30 to 35 minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch and freeze before baking. The filling can be made 2 days ahead.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The filling can be made 2 days ahead and refrigerated. Assemble and bake on the day.

glossaryTerms.definition: The decorative fold or crimp used to seal the edge of an empanada. Different regions of Argentina have their own traditional repulgue styles, and the fold can indicate the filling inside.

content.text: This recipe makes 12 empanadas and takes about 70 minutes. The filling is made first and cooled before assembly, which is important: hot filling makes the pastry soft and hard to work with. If you have shop-bought shortcrust pastry, you can use that to cut the time considerably.
The sealing fold is called a

. The simplest method is to fold the circle in half over the filling and press the edges together firmly, then crimp with a fork. More experienced cooks do a twisted rope crimp that holds better and looks striking. Do not overfill or the empanadas will burst. A heaped tablespoon of filling per pastry is about right.

items.prepNote: one for the dough, one beaten for glazing

content.text: Make the filling first. Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Cook the onion for 8 minutes until soft. Add the garlic, 1 tsp cumin and 1 tsp sweet paprika, cook for 1 minute. Add the minced beef and cook, breaking it up, for 8 minutes until browned. Stir in 8 roughly chopped green olives and season with salt. Leave to cool completely, then stir in 2 chopped hard-boiled eggs.

Make the pastry. Rub the cold butter into the flour until the mixture resembles fine breadcrumbs. Add 1 egg and 3 to 4 tbsp ice-cold water, mixing until the dough just comes together. Do not overwork it. Wrap and rest in the fridge for 20 minutes.
Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan). Line 2 baking trays.
On a lightly floured surface, roll the pastry to about 3mm thick. Cut out 12 circles, roughly 13cm in diameter, using a large cutter or a saucer as a guide.

Place a heaped tablespoon of cooled filling on one half of each circle. Fold the other half over and press the edges firmly to seal. Crimp with a fork or fold over using a twisted rope technique. Place on the lined trays.
Brush each empanada with beaten egg. Bake for 22 to 25 minutes until golden and the pastry is crisp. Cool for 5 minutes before eating.

attrs.symptom: Empanadas are bursting open during baking
attrs.cause: Overfilled, or the edges were not sealed firmly enough
attrs.fix: Use no more than 1 heaped tablespoon of filling. Press the edges firmly together, then crimp with a fork to create a better seal. Make sure the filling is fully cool before assembling.

attrs.cause: Dough was overworked, which develops the gluten and makes it chewy
attrs.fix: Mix the pastry until it just comes together, then stop. Rest it in the fridge before rolling. Overhandling the dough is the main cause of tough pastry.

attrs.cause: Beef was cooked at too high a heat or for too long
attrs.fix: Add a splash of beef stock or water to the filling while it cooks if it looks dry. The filling should be moist but not wet when it goes into the pastry.

content.text: Empanadas are eaten across Argentina at any time of day: as a snack, as a starter at an asado, or as a quick lunch. Each province has its own style. In Salta the filling is spicier and includes potato. In Tucuman they are smaller and eaten in one bite. In Buenos Aires they tend to be larger, with a richer, wetter filling. The debate over which regional style is the best is a serious one in Argentina.
